title: Checkpoint: Nouns, Cases, and the Verb
summary: A cumulative examination of sections seven to nine: the plural and the class system, the case suffixes glued onto the oblique stem, and the verb that agrees in person, number and class.

drills.explanation: -లు is added and the stem is untouched — the simplest of the plural classes.
A noun in -ం gives up its anusvāra for a long vowel: *pustakaṃ → pustakālu*. Nouns of this shape are very numerous.

drills.stem: In the **singular**, which belongs to the మహత్ class?
drills.explanation: Only a male human being. A woman is grammatically amahat in the singular, grouped with the tree and the book — the fact a European learner finds hardest to accept.

drills.stem: You are inviting the person you are speaking to. Which word for **we**?
drills.explanation: మనం includes the hearer, మేము excludes them. English has one word for both and will let you be vague; Telugu will not.

drills.stem: Of **men, women, dogs and books**, how many are మహత్ in the **plural**?
drills.explanation: Two — men and women, together mahat once plural. The same four kinds in the singular would give one, because the line moves between the numbers.
-నుండి, or -నుంచి in speech. -లో is *in*, -తో *with*, -కి the dative.
The oblique stem నా- takes the dative suffix. Adding -కు to the nominative *నేను* gives a form that does not exist — the suffixes are regular and it is the stems that change.

drills.stem: Why does *పుస్తకం* carry no suffix in **నేను పుస్తకం చదువుతున్నాను**, though it is the object?
options: Because the verb is in the present.
Because the object is a lifeless thing, and such an object commonly stands bare.
drills.explanation: The accusative -ని is used chiefly of people and animals. Where the object is lifeless, word order alone shows what it is — a distinction the European accusative does not draw.

drills.stem: Which statements distinguish Telugu from a fusional language such as Lithuanian?
options: Its case suffixes keep one shape across all nouns.
Its suffixes can be separated from the stem.
It fuses case and number into a single indivisible ending.
It places case markers after the noun rather than before.
drills.explanation: Fusing case and number into one ending is exactly what Lithuanian does and Telugu does not: Telugu adds the plural, then the case, each keeping its own shape.

drills.stem: *ఇల్లు* becomes *ఇంటికి* in the dative. What has changed?
options: The suffix, which is irregular for this noun.
The stem, which takes its oblique form ఇంటి- before the regular suffix.
The number, which has become plural.
Nothing; the two are alternative spellings.
drills.explanation: -కి is perfectly regular. It is the stem that changes, and a noun with an unpredictable oblique must be learned with it — as a Lithuanian noun is learned with its genitive.

drills.stem: **నేను ఇంట్లో ఉన్నాను** — how many of its three words carry a case suffix?
drills.explanation: One: *ఇంట్లో*. *నేను* is the bare nominative, which takes no suffix at all, and the third word is the verb. Counting two usually means mistaking the nominative for a marked case.

drills.stem: Where does the verb stand in a Telugu sentence?
drills.explanation: Subject–object–verb. Everything the verb governs comes before it, and the same ordering runs through the language.
-తున్న- is the progressive: the action is going on now. The habitual and the future are both *చదువుతాను*, with -తా-.

drills.stem: Which verb ending goes with **a woman**, singular?
drills.explanation: -ది, the same ending a dog or a book takes. The class division of ¶41 is not a matter of pronouns only: it is written into the verb.

drills.stem: Which of these are correctly matched?
drills.explanation: వాళ్ళు is the human plural and takes -రు, giving *వెళ్ళారు*. -యి belongs to అవి, the non-human plural; putting people there is the commonest agreement error.

drills.stem: How is **I did not go** said?
drills.explanation: లేదు is added to the bare stem and the personal ending drops away. కాదు denies an identity — *this is not a book* — and cannot deny an action.

drills.stem: In what order are the pieces of **చదువుతున్నాను** assembled?
drills.explanation: చదువు + తున్న + ను. The order is fixed and each piece keeps its own shape — which is what being agglutinative means.

drills.stem: How many **distinct personal endings** has the Telugu verb, for its nine pronouns?
drills.explanation: Seven. మేము and మనం share -ము, and మీరు and వాళ్ళు share -రు, so the verb cannot always tell you which pronoun was meant.

drills.stem: How would you say **with a friend**?
drills.explanation: -తో covers both the instrument and the companion, where English divides *written with a pen* from *came with a friend*. The others give *to*, *in* and *from*.

drills.title: మా ఇల్లు
drills.passage: మా ఇల్లు ఒక చిన్న ఊరిలో ఉంది. నేను ఇప్పుడు హైదరాబాద్‌లో ఉన్నాను. నా అక్క ఊరిలో ఉంది. ఆమె రోజూ పని చేస్తుంది. నా అన్నలు కూడా అక్కడ ఉన్నారు. వాళ్ళు రేపు ఇక్కడికి వస్తారు. కుక్కలు ఇంటి బయట ఉన్నాయి. నిన్న నేను ఊరికి వెళ్ళలేదు.
drills.translation: Our house is in a small village. I am now in Hyderabad. My elder sister is in the village. She works every day. My elder brothers are also there. They will come here tomorrow. The dogs are outside the house. Yesterday I did not go to the village.

questions.explanation: *నా అక్క ఊరిలో ఉంది* — the locative -లో marks where she is. Hyderabad is where the speaker is.

questions.stem: Which of these does the passage support?
questions.explanation: The dogs are *ఇంటి బయట*, outside the house, not in it. Note the three endings the passage sets side by side: -ఆరు for the brothers, -ఆయి for the dogs, and లేదు with no ending at all for the denial.

questions.stem: The passage has **నా అక్క ఊరిలో ఉంది.** If it spoke of two sisters instead of one, how many words would change form?
questions.explanation: Two: *అక్క* becomes plural, and the verb with it — *ఉంది* → *ఉన్నారు*, the amahat singular ending giving way to the mahat plural one, because a woman changes class on becoming plural (¶42, ¶53). *నా* is indeclinable and *ఊరిలో* is untouched. Answering one forgets that the verb carries the class.
